claims.claim: The first big forecast search found 1,217 forecast recipes worth trusting.
claims.maker: Our forecast program, first search
claims.result: Only 63 of the 1,217 earned the top grade on the second look. 337 held up, 564 did not reproduce at all, and 253 could not be tested. The book of promoted recipes was frozen at 388 entries.
claims.sample: 1,217 recipes re-graded
claims.study: A second search, planned and written down before it ran, re-grading every one of the 1,217 recipes on a second set of data

claims.claim: The named setup families are good enough to trade live.
claims.maker: Our setup picker, checked against the forecast program's replay
claims.result: No setup family passed the go-live bar. The replay was itself reproduced case for case by a second run: its best family row scored an edge of +0.081 (range 0.029 to 0.133), and its baseline row scored -0.025.
claims.sample: 296,093 replayed cases across 9 family definitions
claims.study: A replay of every historical case the picker would have taken, checked family by family against a go-live bar set in advance

claims.claim: A mechanical bull-flag breakout is the only setup you need: it makes money on its own.
claims.maker: Casey (@Team2Trading), a trading educator
claims.result: It lost 0.0345% per trade after costs, with a strength score of -3.56 (past -2 is strong evidence, in the losing direction). It also lost on the SPY and IWM checks, and none of 6 variations of the rule changed the sign.
claims.sample: 611 trades over 677 trading days (QQQ, 2-minute bars, January 2, 2024 to October 5, 2026)
claims.study: A frozen, pre-written test of the exact mechanical rule, run by us on index data

claims.claim: Those bull-flag breaks can double a same-day call option, up over 100%.
claims.maker: Casey (@Team2Trading), a trading educator
claims.result: Only 4.3% of breaks moved far enough in the right direction to double a call; the claim needed 25%. The middle break moved just +0.026% before costs.
claims.sample: 611 mechanical breaks
claims.study: The same frozen bull-flag study, checking how far each break actually travelled

claims.claim: Adding a 13/48 moving-average filter makes the bull flag better.
claims.maker: Casey (@Team2Trading), a trading educator
claims.result: Cannot be tested on the records on hand. Re-reading every trade on the study's record: the 589 filtered trades averaged -0.36 of their risk unit and the 22 unfiltered trades averaged -0.75, a difference in the filter's favour with a strength score of 1.34, below the 2.0 bar. The missing record is a sample of filter-rejected trades large enough to decide the comparison: the filter passes 96% of its own signals, so that sample would have to come from other symbols or other years, and no such record is on hand.
claims.sample: 611 trades on the record, 589 passing the filter and 22 not passing it
claims.study: The frozen bull-flag study's own per trade record, re-read in full for this wire
claims.verdict_words: Cannot be tested on the records on hand
claims.when: Study finished October 2026; per trade record re-read October 30, 2026

claims.claim: A multi-timeframe VWAP trend stack is a high-probability intraday trade.
claims.maker: Anand (@TradesByAnand), a trading educator
claims.result: The breakout arm lost 0.026% per trade after costs, and lost 0.156% per trade in the held-back years. It could not beat random entries in the same stocks (strength score -0.06 against random). The study's own verdict: dead on the intraday horizon.
claims.sample: 251 breakout trades over 1,699 trading days (January 2, 2020 to October 6, 2026)
claims.study: A pre-registered test of the full stack in the 20 most liquid large stocks, run by us

claims.claim: Strong volume plus an RSI above 50 add edge to that VWAP stack.
claims.maker: Anand (@TradesByAnand), a trading educator
claims.result: On breakouts, confirmed trades did worse than unconfirmed ones by 0.015% per trade (strength -0.53). On retests they did better by 0.054% (strength 1.73), below the +0.10% bar set before the test ran.
claims.sample: 251 breakout trades and 19 retest trades
claims.study: The same pre-registered VWAP study, comparing trades with and without the two confirmations

claims.claim: The same VWAP stack works if you hold for days instead of hours.
claims.maker: Anand (@TradesByAnand), a trading educator
claims.result: Cannot be tested on the records on hand. On the windows the study spent, the swing arms were too small to decide (they could only have spotted an edge of 0.242% or 0.360% per trade, against a 0.20% ceiling). The missing record is the study's sealed final test set: its own written protocol forbids opening it before the earlier windows render a go verdict, they never did, and no ruling has opened it since.
claims.sample: 251 swing breakout trades and 19 swing retest trades on the spent windows
claims.study: The swing arms of the same pre-registered VWAP study
claims.verdict_words: Cannot be tested on the records on hand
claims.when: Study dated October 6, 2026; protocol re-read October 30, 2026

claims.claim: The textbook pullback, buying a dip to the 20/50-day lines in an uptrend, earns money.
claims.maker: Trading-education sellers generally; the pattern is a staple of their courses
claims.result: It earned +0.05 of its risk unit per trade, no better than random entries in the same stocks (+0.08) or random days inside uptrends (+0.03).
claims.sample: About 85,000 trades across 6,385 stocks including delisted ones, 2016 to 2026
claims.study: An independent cross-check on deep price history, run by our research program

claims.claim: Buying dips in uptrends, a touch of the 20-day line with a trend filter, is a working strategy.
claims.maker: A strategy question we set ourselves
claims.result: In the held-back years it shrank money at 37.8% a year, with a strength score of -18.26 against picking random days instead. All 4 versions of the trigger failed the same way. The study's verdict: kill it.
claims.sample: 278,090 trades across 1,838 stocks, 2016 to 2026
claims.study: A walk-forward test (rules fixed in advance, tested on later years) across the full stock list

claims.claim: Buying washed-out pullbacks to support in uptrending AI stocks pays better, per unit of fall, than simply holding the semiconductor fund SMH.
claims.maker: Our AI top-50 pattern study, written up as a pre-registered test
claims.result: It grew at 9.84% a year with a worst fall of 27.25%: 0.361 of return per unit of fall, against SMH's 0.716. It failed 2 of its 4 pre-set marks and all 11 variations (best 0.517). It did pass its bear-market mark: its worst fall in the bear stretch was 1.21% against SMH's 45.30%, because it sat in cash on 98.66% of bear days.
claims.sample: 60 trades, October 25, 2021 to October 23, 2026
claims.study: A pre-registered backtest with its pass marks set before it ran

claims.claim: Buying the past year's winners, long-only time-series momentum, beats picking stocks at random.
claims.maker: A textbook claim, in the form a popular chart account published it
claims.result: Half the claim held: the strongest-decile version's return per unit of fall was 0.58 in the held-back years, which clears its bar, and it scored a strength of 3.47 in the development years. But against random picks its strength was only 0.68, below the 2.0 bar, and the sealed final test (December 2024 to August 2026) has never been opened, so the verdict stays parked, neither proven nor buried. A known data fault pushes that 0.68 down; a sensitivity check bounds the corrected figure near 2.09.
claims.sample: 1,838 stocks, 2016 to 2026, at 0.75% trading costs
claims.study: A clean re-run on repaired data, after an earlier run was found to rest on faulty data

claims.claim: How deep a pullback is, compared with that stock's own normal pullback size, ranks what the stock does next.
claims.maker: Our own cross-check: a new candidate ranking found by the research program
claims.note: One study, counted once: the forecast program's own plan for a fear-day ranking prints these same two numbers for it, because fear days are part of this same study. The study record itself attaches the numbers to the pullback-depth ranking.
claims.result: The ranking pointed the same way in both eras: its agreement with later 20-day returns scored +0.026 in the first era and +0.031 in the second (strength 4.3 both times), and +0.062 at 60 days in the second era (strength 9.8). That is a real pattern on one family of data, still an unproven candidate, not a validated edge.
claims.sample: Deep price history, 2016 to 2026, fear days included
claims.study: A cross-check on deep price history, tested separately in two eras, 2016 to 2022 and 2023 onward

claims.claim: The rebuilt confluence board's 0-to-100 score ranks the returns that follow.
claims.maker: A vendor's confluence design (Leadr), rebuilt by us with its settings verbatim and our own scoring arithmetic
claims.result: The score's ranking agreed with later returns not at all: the rank agreement was -0.014 at 1 day, -0.021 at 5 days and -0.010 at 21 days, which is zero for practical purposes.
claims.sample: 52,968 scored rows over 29 weekly dates, April 8 to October 23, 2026
claims.study: A backtest of every scored week on record

claims.claim: Even if the score does not rank, the board's pass-every-check gate picks better stocks.
claims.maker: The same rebuilt confluence board
claims.result: At 21 days the passed group averaged +2.41% against +0.52% for the rest (+0.61% against the S&P 500 fund, versus -1.12%). But its middle stock did worse than the fund at every horizon (-0.16%, -0.36%, -1.16%): the average is carried by a right tail of big winners, over one 6.5-month window.
claims.sample: 52,968 scored rows over 29 weekly dates, April 8 to October 23, 2026
claims.study: The same backtest, comparing the stocks that passed every check with the rest

claims.claim: The board's live published stock calls rise more often than not after 1 day.
claims.maker: Our own published board, graded live
claims.result: So far, early and small: 88 published calls graded at 1 day, 52% rose, averaging -0.10%. The pass-every-check group: 47 graded, 55% rose, averaging -0.09%. The 5-day grades first land after the October 30, 2026 close and the 21-day grades after the November 23, 2026 close.
claims.sample: 88 published calls graded at 1 day so far
claims.study: The live grading record for every call the board has published, re-read fresh for this page

claims.claim: Big options walls hold, and the level where the picture flips is respected.
claims.maker: A published positioning construction (SpotGamma's), rebuilt and graded by us
claims.result: A tiny sample, stated as counts: the upper wall held on 8 of 12 cards, the lower wall held on 11 of 12, and the flip level was respected on 12 of 12.
claims.sample: 12 index cards graded so far
claims.study: The live grading record for the published index positioning cards

claims.claim: A chart ranker's 0.736 ranking agreement is a forecasting result.
claims.maker: The ChartsLector chart-ranking lane
claims.result: Ruled not a prediction: the 0.736 measures agreement with one fitted 55-name vendor snapshot, not agreement with future returns, and it was reached only after three rotation mistakes and a split-adjustment fault in the ranker's data were corrected.
claims.sample: One fitted snapshot of 55 names from the vendor
claims.study: An audit of the ranker and its data, inside our research analysis

claims.claim: TheStrat's posted proof, its trade recaps, backs its rule system.
claims.maker: TheStrat, a trading-rules vendor
claims.result: Cannot be tested on the records on hand: the teardown is the largest rule extraction in our research files and carries zero test entries and zero evidence entries, and its one posted proof item is a single trade recap (+$337.02, -21%), one anecdote, not a test. The missing record is any graded record of the system's own calls (a test or evidence entry for the rule system); none exists in the teardown or anywhere else on hand.
claims.sample: 3,615 teardown entries examined
claims.study: Our evidence audit of the vendor's full teardown
claims.verdict_words: Cannot be tested on the records on hand
claims.when: Evidence audit finished October 2026; re-read October 30, 2026

claims.claim: The big bundle products' mechanisms work as sold.
claims.maker: Nansen, FlashAlpha, OptionsCartel, GexRadar, TapeBoard and TradeEcho
claims.result: Cannot be tested on the records on hand: the share of each teardown that is tests or evidence is 0.7% for Nansen (3,535 entries), 0.1% for FlashAlpha (2,047) and OptionsCartel (1,942), and 0.2% for GexRadar (2,338), TapeBoard (2,560) and TradeEcho (2,042), with zero tests in each. The missing record is a test record for even one named mechanism per product that this wire could re-run; the teardowns describe mechanisms but carry no test entries, so there is nothing on hand to test the claim against. Their mechanisms are unproven either way, not disproven.
claims.sample: Six teardowns, 2,042 to 3,535 entries each
claims.study: Our evidence audit of each vendor's teardown
claims.verdict_words: Cannot be tested on the records on hand
claims.when: Evidence audit finished October 2026; re-read October 30, 2026

claims.claim: The 15.87 expected-move formula (the day's expected move equals the close times the fear gauge divided by 15.87) reproduces its author's own published values.
claims.maker: Azrael Options, author of the 15.87 rule
claims.result: It reproduces the author's own values exactly: expected moves of 73.0 and 81.5, and a weekly move of 182.2, and every filed map recomputes exactly. This grades the calculation only: it says nothing about whether trading on the move makes money.
claims.sample: The author's published example values, plus every filed map on record
claims.study: Our rebuild of the formula, checked against the author's own worked examples and every filed map

claims.claim: Nine rebuilt vendor calculators give the same answers as hand-worked examples.
claims.maker: A second, independent rebuild of several trading calculators
claims.result: All 9 of 9 cases pass, with the sources for each case pinned by fingerprint in the results. This grades the calculators' arithmetic against worked examples, not any trading claim.
claims.sample: 9 hand-worked cases
claims.study: Hand-worked test cases for each calculator, including a positioning measure built from a hand-computed option formula, a spread payoff priced at three prices, and a confluence score

claims.claim: Two independent rebuilds of the same vendor mechanisms agree with each other.
claims.maker: Our calculator engine and the second independent rebuild, cross-checked by us
claims.result: 11 cases agree and are pinned as tests. Every disagreement is named: two were faults in our engine, fixed at the source; two were ruled faults in the second rebuild, on the vendor's own published evidence; and the cases only one rebuild covers were left uncovered, not papered over.
claims.sample: Every case where both rebuilds cover the same mechanism
claims.study: A cross-check: one rebuild's test cases run against the other rebuild, case by case

claims.claim: TheStrat's 71-rule bar-labelling system can be rebuilt faithfully from its published rules.
claims.maker: Our replica of the vendor's published rules
claims.result: The replica passes 21 of 21 tests. This grades whether the labels match the published rules; whether following the system makes money is untested, and its forward record does not exist yet.
claims.sample: 21 tests, including the vendor's own example cases
claims.study: A working replica tested against the rule set, including the vendor's own worked examples

claims.claim: Golden sweep prints, a sweep at least as large as its contract's whole open interest with at least $1 million in it, are a signal worth following.
claims.maker: An options-tape vendor tag, rebuilt by us
claims.result: Cannot be tested on the records on hand: two golden prints stand on the recorded sessions, but neither has the following sessions a grade needs, so there is nothing gradeable yet. The missing record is the rest of the tape its own decision rule requires: 25 more recorded sessions to reach 30, with the decision date already set at December 8, 2026. Until a golden print's following sessions exist, no verdict either way is possible.
claims.sample: 5 recorded trading days so far on the index tape record, freshest session October 30, 2026, with two golden prints found
claims.study: Our recording of every options print on the three index funds, checked for golden sweeps
claims.verdict_words: Cannot be tested on the records on hand
claims.when: Recording started October 2026; tape record recounted October 30, 2026

claims.claim: The forecast program's one-verdict-per-stock router (Buy, Wait, Avoid, or Sit Out) has a track record.
claims.maker: Our forecast program
claims.result: Cannot be tested on the records on hand: its record is 7 sessions and provisional, and the program's own plan requires its card to say exactly that, in words, until the record grows up. The missing record is a graded track record for this router: sessions of its verdicts with their outcomes graded against what the stocks did next, in the number its own maturity bar requires. No graded record for it exists on hand.
claims.sample: 7 trading sessions of record, none of them graded
claims.study: The router's own published record so far
claims.verdict_words: Cannot be tested on the records on hand
claims.when: Record as of October 2026; re-read October 30, 2026

claims.claim: Overnight gaps usually fill.
claims.maker: A common trading saying, measured by our gap study
claims.result: Not usually: 83 of 186 gaps filled (44.6%). By size: gaps under 1% filled 82 of 168 (48.8%), and gaps of 1 to 2% filled only 1 of 18 (5.6%).
claims.sample: 186 gap cases graded
claims.study: Our gap study: every overnight gap in the index funds on record, checked for a same-day fill

explanation.body: On its live record it counts 11 did not, 3 held, 7 partly, 27 total. No study record is on file for this page; what it shows is its current reading, updated on its normal schedule.
